back: A continuous network of a very large number of atoms joined by strong covalent bonds, with no separate small molecules.
Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others (tetrahedrally) in a rigid three-dimensional network; no free electrons.
Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three others in flat hexagonal layers; weak forces between layers; one delocalised electron per atom.

front: Why is diamond used in cutting tools?
back: It is extremely hard, because every atom is held by four strong covalent bonds in a 3D network.

front: Why is graphite used as a lubricant?
back: The forces between its layers are weak, so the layers slide over each other easily.

front: Why is graphite used for electrodes?
back: It conducts electricity (delocalised electrons move along the layers) and has a very high melting point.

front: Why does graphite conduct electricity but diamond does not?
back: Graphite uses three of each atom's four outer electrons in bonds, leaving one delocalised; diamond uses all four, so it has no free electrons.

front: Why do diamond and graphite both have very high melting points?
back: Melting means breaking many strong covalent bonds in the giant structure, which needs a lot of energy.

front: **Supplement.** Describe the structure of silicon(IV) oxide, $\ce{SiO2}$.
back: A giant covalent 3D network: each Si bonded to four O atoms and each O bonded to two Si atoms (ratio 1 : 2).

front: **Supplement.** Why is silicon(IV) oxide like diamond in its properties?
back: Both are 3D giant covalent structures with many strong covalent bonds and no free electrons: hard, high melting point, non-conducting, insoluble.
